title: A Moon-phase bias near the ZTF detection limit explains the 30-day signal of SN 2020sgf, and SN Ia controls pass a periodicity test as often as stripped-envelope supernovae
abstract: Question: Are the 30-day periodic modulations reported in ZTF light curves of stripped-envelope supernovae (SESN; Horowicz, Ofek and Gal-Yam 2026) caused by the Moon or by the test? Method: We used ZTF public alert photometry (ALeRCE) of 2,921 Bright Transient Survey supernovae, 2018-2026. We regressed decline residuals on Moon illumination and compared them with a simulation of the 5-sigma detection cut. We repeated the cubic-plus-sinusoid periodicity rule of Horowicz et al. on 1,426 light curves, with a Moon term, a degree-5 baseline and a white-noise bootstrap, and compared SESN with normal SN Ia and SN II controls. Results: Near the detection limit, SNe look brighter at full Moon only when the Moon is up (-0.19 +- 0.02 mag per unit illumination, simulation -0.23 +- 0.02). This is selection by the shallower limit. More than 1.5 mag above the limit, the Moon effect is within +-0.02 mag. Best fits at 25-38 d lock to the Moon phase (181 of 294 brighter at full Moon, p = 9e-5), but not with bright points only or with a Moon term. For SN 2020sgf, a degree-5 baseline gives 29.4-30.0 d in phase with the Moon (r = -0.97, -0.99), and one Moon term removes the signal. Two-band 'periodic' detections occur in SNe Ia (0-9 percent for different baselines) at about the published SESN rate (8.8 percent). With a degree-5 baseline and a Moon term, SESN give 1/53 (SN 2022jli) and SNe Ia 1/90. SN 2022jli (12.5 d) is robust. SN 2022esa (33-36 d, bright points) is not explained by the Moon and stays open. Limitations: alert photometry, not forced photometry; no independent survey (ATLAS) test; low sensitivity to 0.07 mag signals, so a periodic SESN sub-population is not excluded.
